name: Swanson's Law
statement: Solar module prices fall about 20% for every doubling of cumulative shipped volume.
statementAccent: for every doubling of cumulative shipped volume
meaning: Swanson's law is the observation that the price of solar photovoltaic modules tends to fall by about twenty percent for every doubling of cumulative shipped volume. It is a solar-specific instance of the experience or learning curve, keyed to how much has ever been produced rather than to the passage of time. A commonly cited corollary is that, at the growth rates of recent decades, costs have fallen by around three-quarters roughly every ten years. The figure is a rough regularity, with estimates clustering near twenty percent, not an exact constant.
mechanism: The law is the experience curve applied to solar photovoltaics. As cumulative production doubles, accumulated manufacturing experience improves yields and processes, larger factories and supply chains lower unit costs for polysilicon, wafers, and cells, and technology advances raise cell efficiency and use less silicon and silver per watt. The twenty percent drop per doubling corresponds to a learning rate of about twenty percent, or an eighty percent progress ratio, in the language of learning curves. Because the driver is cumulative volume, the effect requires production to keep doubling, and each doubling takes longer as the industry matures.

examples.text: Crystalline-silicon module prices fell from roughly seventy-six dollars per watt in 1977 to well under a dollar by around 2012 and to a few tens of cents in the 2020s, a decline of over ninety-nine percent.
Solar costs fell far faster than most official energy projections for over a decade, a now-classic case of forecasters underestimating a learning-curve technology.
Modules dropping below a dollar per watt of capacity around 2012 was the point The Economist flagged in naming the law after Richard Swanson.

variants.name: The experience curve
variants.text: The general principle, from the Boston Consulting Group, that unit costs fall a constant percentage per doubling of cumulative production; Swanson's law is its solar-specific form.

variants.name: Contrast with Moore's law
variants.text: Moore's law is roughly time-based, a doubling every couple of years, whereas Swanson's law is keyed to cumulative volume, so the 'cheaper every decade' figure is a consequence of past volume growth, not a fixed clock.

whyItMatters: It captured a fall in solar costs that mainstream energy forecasters repeatedly and dramatically underestimated, reframing solar from a niche, subsidy-dependent technology into one increasingly cost-competitive with or cheaper than fossil fuels for new generation. That reshaped energy-transition and climate modelling and gave a deployment-driven basis for projecting future costs: policies that grow cumulative volume mechanically drive price down. It has become a standard reference point in debates over how fast renewable energy can scale.

working.text: project module price from cumulative shipped volume rather than from the calendar, since the doubling of production is what drives the fall.
anticipate each doubling taking longer as the industry matures, so annual price declines ease even as the curve continues.
remember that module price is only part of an installed system's cost, so a module drop does not translate one-for-one to cheaper rooftop solar.

limits: It is an empirical trend, not a physical law, a fitted regularity with scatter around the twenty percent line and no guarantee of continuing. It depends on cumulative volume continuing to double, and as the industry matures each doubling takes longer while material and processing floors constrain further drops; forecasters now project only a few percent annual module-price decline, versus fifteen to twenty percent in the prior decade, consistent with a slowing rather than repealed curve. Module price is also only part of total system cost: balance-of-system and soft costs such as inverters, mounting, labour, and permitting have not fallen nearly as fast. The learning rate itself is uncertain, around twenty to twenty-five percent.
misreadings: It is not like Moore's law and not about time: Moore's law is roughly time-based, while Swanson's law is keyed to cumulative volume, and the 'cheaper every decade' figure is a derived consequence of past volume growth, not a fundamental clock. It is not twenty percent cheaper every year; the twenty percent is per doubling of cumulative volume, which only coincided with near-annual declines while volume was doubling fast. It governs module price, not the price of a whole installed system, which includes large non-module costs. And Swanson did not invent it in 2012; The Economist popularised the name then, over an older underlying relationship.
origin: Named after Richard Swanson, founder of SunPower, who had long presented such solar cost curves; the name was popularised by The Economist around 2012, and it is a solar-specific case of the experience curve traceable to Theodore Wright's 1936 learning curve.

sources.text: Swanson's law, Wikipedia. — the ~20 percent per doubling statement, the price history, and the naming by The Economist.
